_about: The command-line contract of every installed host tool, in one place.
test_cli_matrix.py reads this file and generates the cases from it, so a
rule written here is checked against the real binaries rather than
described in prose only.
JSON rather than YAML on purpose: the test runs on CI images that have
python3 and nothing else (the Ubuntu 20.04 and Fedora containers install
python3 alone), and PyYAML is not among them.
Where this file and a tool disagree, the disagreement is a finding, listed
in "expected_failures" with its finding id, not a rule bent to match the
code. Where the man page does not decide a case, it is listed in
"undecided" with a question id and only the universal checks run.

_verdicts.help: the usage text on stdout, exit 0, stderr empty, no device looked for
_verdicts.report: the answer on stdout, exit 0, stderr empty (-V notes a board in the DFU bootloader there, which no run of this test has)
_verdicts.silent_success: exit 0 and both streams empty: a command that only set something, which the codebase reports by saying nothing, or one whose answer is that it has nothing to say (btle-extcap.py verifying an empty capture filter)
_verdicts.count_only: a decimal count on stdout, exit 0, no device opened
_verdicts.count_then_device: the count on stdout first, then the rest of the command reaches device lookup
_verdicts.usage: the one 'error: ' line then the usage text, both on stderr, exit 1, stdout empty, no device looked for
_verdicts.refused: exactly one 'error: ' line on stderr, exit 1, stdout empty, no usage text, no device looked for
_verdicts.device: the command line was accepted, so the run reaches device lookup: exit 1 with the device-lookup message on stderr
_verdicts.report_then_help: both answers on stdout, the report first and the usage text last, exit 0, stderr empty, no device looked for
_verdicts.undecided: only the universal checks: a valid exit status, and either a clean refusal or device lookup

_universal: the exit status is 0 or 1, or a code the tool's man page lists
stdout is empty whenever the status is not 0, unless the option is listed in stdout_on_failure
a refusal is exactly one line starting 'error: ' on stderr
the usage text appears on stdout only for -h, and on stderr only after a bare command line
a refused command line never reaches device lookup
a refused command line creates no file
_local_adapter_probe: ubertooth-follow and ubertooth-scan open the local Bluetooth adapter
before they look for an Ubertooth, so where an accepted command line
stops depends on whether the machine has one. The test runs the bare
command once to find out: an "accepted_markers" message means there is
no adapter, and every accepted case stops there. With an adapter present
those cases would go on to talk to it, which is not what this test is
about, so they are skipped, the run says how many, and the findings
Either way, what those two tools do after the adapter opens is outside
this matrix: on a machine with no adapter they stop at it, and on one
with an adapter the accepted cases are not run. Lines they print past
that point are unchecked, and ubertooth-follow.c and ubertooth-scan.c
do print some of them on stdout, so this is a gap and not a clean
result. Closing it needs a fake adapter, which is a job of its own.

_about: What an option is, in one word. test_cli_matrix.py acts on four of
these by name -- "help" and "report" end the command, "selector"
names a board, and "modifier" is what an option without a role gets
-- and any of them, those four included, can be a pair rule's side as
"role:<name>". A name that is not here selects nothing, so every role
an option carries is checked against this table, every name here has
to be carried by an option, and a rule's "role:" side has to name a
role the options it applies to carry.
_roles.help: prints the usage text and ends the command
_roles.report: answers and ends the command, like -h
_roles.selector: names the board the command runs on
_roles.modifier: changes how the work is done, rather than being work of its own
_roles.work: work of its own, rather than a setting for other work
_roles.major_mode: picks what the tool does, so two of them together is a mode clash
_roles.mode: a mode ubertooth-util puts the board into
_roles.action: makes the board do something once (a reset, or stopping what it is doing)
_roles.query: reads a value out of the board and prints it
_roles.setter: writes a setting to the board, or reads it back when the value is left off
_roles.count: counts the boards attached, which needs no board opened
_roles.target: names the address the command follows
_roles.address: sets the access address a capture listens for
_roles.channel: sets the channel the run uses
_roles.range: one end of the frequency range a sweep covers
_roles.capture: writes what was captured to a file, or to standard output for a lone "-"
_roles.replay: replays a capture from a file instead of taking one
_roles.verify: checks the packets it captured rather than only recording them
_roles.survey: collects a survey of what is on the air rather than printing packets
_roles.afh_read: reads the target's hop pattern rather than following it
_roles.faux_slave: answers as a slave rather than listening
_roles.interfere: transmits at the target rather than capturing it
_roles.modulation: picks the modulation a capture is read as
_roles.output_mode: picks the form the samples are printed in
_roles.undocumented: an option the tool's man page does not list

_global_pair_rules.why: -h and -V both end the command and both answer on standard output, so a line with both prints both: the version first and the usage text last, whichever order they were written in (.kiro/steering/cli-output.md). The first one written used to win and the other was dropped.
-h ends the command whatever else the line asks for, once the whole line has parsed
-V answers the version and ends the command, like -h

_shape: The installed wrapper host/python/ubtbr/ubertooth-btbr.in, built by
CMake. It finds its board through the Python usb1 module rather than
libubertooth, so the matrix gives it a usb1 that finds nothing
instead of setting UBERTOOTH_TEST_NO_DEVICES; its -U selection is
the ubtbr module's own, checked against several fake boards by
host/python/ubtbr/tests/test_ubtbr.py. The interactive prompt is not
a command line and is covered by the same test.

error: advertising channel index must be 37-39 (got 40)

cases.why: Wireshark verifying a capture filter: the filter and an interface, with no operation. What this call writes to standard output is the answer, which Wireshark shows in the capture filter box, so it goes there and the call exits 0; a non-zero exit would make Wireshark discard the answer.
the empty filter Wireshark verifies when the box is empty is good, and an empty standard output is what says so

why_not: The script imports numpy and a Qt binding at module level, before it
reads its command line, so none of its refusals can be reached on a
machine without them. Its own test
What it would check: -h on stdout with status 0, and one 'error: '
line on stderr with status 1 for a bad -l/-u range, a --wifi channel
that is not 1-14 and a --padding that is not a whole number of MHz,
all before the window opens (ubertooth-specan-ui.md ARGUMENTS).

_about: Where a tool and the rules disagree. Each one is listed in
"expected_failures" as the cases it breaks and every complaint they
produce, one entry in "problem_contains" per complaint. Every case
listed has to keep failing in all of those ways, so a finding fixed
for some of its cases, or breaking in one fewer way, fails this test
rather than passing quietly.
There are none: every case in the matrix states what the tool is to
do and the tools do it.
Cases the man pages never decide. The test runs them and checks only
that the tool either refuses cleanly or goes on to look for a device;
which of the two it should be is the maintainer's call.
There are none open: every case carries the verdict it is held to.
